findings.title: SQL injection in vehicle label search
findings.evidence: String.format interpolates tenantId and the raw `label` query parameter into the WHERE clause ('%s' and ILIKE '%%%s%%'), then passes the finished string to prepareStatement with no bind variables. `label` arrives from VehicleController.search @QueryValue at line 58 with no @Pattern, no allowlist and no escaping.
findings.impact: Any authenticated caller can terminate the string literal and rewrite the query: read every tenant's vehicles, UNION other tables, or use Postgres stacked semantics available to the app role. Tenant isolation collapses because tenant_id is itself inside the injectable literal.
findings.recommendation: Bind both values: `WHERE tenant_id = ? AND label ILIKE ?` with the wildcards added to the parameter value, not the SQL.

triage.reason: label is an unvalidated @QueryValue at VehicleController.java:58; nothing constrains it between the handler and the format call.
TenantFilter (TenantFilter.java:19) only sets a request attribute; no filter, interceptor or ORM layer rewrites this SQL string.

scope.established_by: grep for SQL keywords adjacent to concatenation/interpolation across the tree (12 hits), then callers of searchByLabel (1: VehicleController.search)
scope.narrowed_by: @Secured(SecurityRule.IS_AUTHENTICATED) at VehicleController.java:30 - a valid bearer token is required; no role is.

findings.title: OBD frame and fault queries take a tenant id and never use it
findings.evidence: recentFrames (line 132) and openFaults (line 145) both accept a tenantId parameter, and neither SQL statement references tenant_id: `WHERE vehicle_id = ?` and `WHERE vehicle_id = ? AND cleared_at IS NULL`. The sibling statements in the same class (listOrdered:42, update:104, delete:123) all carry `tenant_id = ?`.
findings.impact: Any authenticated user of any tenant who knows or guesses a vehicle id reads that vehicle's live OBD-II telemetry and open fault codes. Vehicle ids are UUIDs returned in this tenant's own listings and in error paths; a UUID is not an access control.
findings.recommendation: Join obd_frames/obd_faults to vehicles and filter on tenant_id, or add tenant_id to those tables and bind it. Delete the unused parameter rather than leaving a signature that looks scoped.

triage.reason: No mandatory layer supplies the filter: TenantFilter.java:19 does not match /api/diagnostics/**, and the DiagnosticsController passes whatever the attribute holds (null) straight through.
The rows are per-vehicle telemetry and fault history belonging to another operator's fleet, which is the data this service exists to keep separated.

scope.established_by: read every SQL string in VehicleRepository and compared which ones bind tenant_id; then listed the two callers in DiagnosticsController

findings.title: Tenant filter covers three route prefixes and not the fourth
findings.evidence: The filter is registered for {"/api/vehicles/**", "/api/depots/**", "/api/trips/**"}. DiagnosticsController is mounted at /api/diagnostics (DiagnosticsController.java:21), which matches none of them - verified by evaluating the three glob patterns against /api/diagnostics/{id}/frames. The controller then reads request.getAttribute("tenantId").orElse(null) (lines 34, 40), so the value the filter exists to establish is simply null there, and the FORBIDDEN branch at TenantFilter.java:38 never runs for those routes.
findings.impact: The one control that is documented as pinning every request to the caller's tenant ('a depot operator can never reach another operator's fleet no matter what they send', lines 16-18) does not apply to the highest-volume controller in the service. Combined with the unscoped queries above, /api/diagnostics is a cross-tenant read surface. The X-Fleet-Tenant strip at line 34 is also skipped for these routes.
findings.recommendation: Register the filter on /api/** (or annotate controllers rather than enumerating prefixes) and make the missing tenant attribute a hard failure in the controllers, not an Optional.orElse(null).

triage.reason: application.yml intercept-url-map (lines 35-37) requires isAuthenticated() on /api/**, which is authentication, not tenant scoping; no other filter exists in the tree.
The gap is the reverse of a narrowing: the construct applies to less than the codebase assumes, which is what makes it a defect rather than a decoy.

findings.title: Effective role is read from a client-supplied header
findings.class: Privilege escalation / trusting client input for authorization
findings.evidence: effectiveRole returns request.getHeaders().get("X-Fleet-Role") whenever the value is one of KNOWN_ROLES, before ever consulting the token. isFleetAdmin (line 34) is built on it and is the only gate on DELETE /api/vehicles/{id} (VehicleController.java:79). TenantFilter removes X-Fleet-Tenant (line 34) and does not remove X-Fleet-Role - in-tree evidence that the authors expect client-supplied copies of these headers to arrive, and that only one of the two is stripped.
findings.impact: A caller holding any valid token adds `X-Fleet-Role: fleet_admin` and deletes vehicles in their tenant regardless of their real role. The gap is wider on /api/diagnostics, where TenantFilter does not run at all.
findings.recommendation: Resolve the role only from the authenticated principal. If the edge must forward it, verify a signature over the header at the service boundary and strip the raw header for every route, not just the three the filter matches.

triage.reason: application.yml:49-54 asserts in prose that the edge re-signs X-Fleet-Tenant/Role/Request-Id, but no gateway configuration, ingress manifest or network policy was provided; per FP-08 an unevidenced external control is UNKNOWN, which caps this at probable.
The in-repo filter strips only X-Fleet-Tenant (TenantFilter.java:34) and only on /api/vehicles|depots|trips; nothing in the tree removes or validates X-Fleet-Role.

scope.established_by: listed every caller of RoleResolver.isFleetAdmin/effectiveRole (one: VehicleController.delete) and compared it against the @Secured-annotated route
scope.narrowed_by: VehicleController.java:87 - pushFirmware uses @Secured("fleet_admin"), which Micronaut evaluates against the token's roles rather than this resolver, so that route is not reachable through the header

findings.title: Command injection in the firmware verifier
findings.evidence: `command` is assembled by concatenation and handed to `new ProcessBuilder("/bin/sh", "-c", command)`. deviceSerial reaches it from VehicleController.FirmwarePush (line 107) carrying only @NotBlank. Its sibling bundleName carries @Pattern("[A-Za-z0-9_.-]{1,48}") (line 106); I evaluated that pattern and it rejects `; id` and `$(id)` - deviceSerial has no such constraint.
findings.impact: A caller who passes the fleet_admin check executes arbitrary commands as the service account on the host holding the firmware staging directory and the signing/verification tooling.
findings.recommendation: Drop the shell: ProcessBuilder(List.of(verifyCommand, "--bundle", path, "--device", deviceSerial)). Apply the same @Pattern to deviceSerial as a second line of defence.

triage.reason: deviceSerial is a request body field validated only by @NotBlank at VehicleController.java:107.
The guard at FirmwareService.java:48 returns early when env != 'production'; the vulnerable branch is precisely the production one, so the shipped production path is the exposed path.
The narrowing that does exist (@Secured fleet_admin) restricts who, not what: the whole tail of the string is still shell-interpreted.

scope.established_by: grep for ProcessBuilder/Runtime.exec//bin/sh across the tree (1 hit), then the single caller of verifyForDevice
scope.narrowed_by: FirmwareService.java:48 (`env` must be 'production'; application.yml:48 defaults FLEET_ENV to staging) and VehicleController.java:87 (@Secured("fleet_admin"))

findings.title: Vehicle update accepts a depot the create path refuses
findings.class: Authorization checked on the path object, not the body object
findings.unaided_label: update() skips depotBelongsTo that create() enforces
findings.evidence: create (line 63) calls vehicles.depotBelongsTo(body.depotId(), tenantId) and returns FORBIDDEN when it fails. update (line 72) takes the same VehicleForm, whose depotId names another row, and writes it straight through: VehicleRepository.update sets `depot_id = ?` (line 103) with no ownership test. The comment on line 73 says the row 'is scoped to the caller's tenant by the update statement' - true of the vehicle, not of the depot it is being moved to.
findings.impact: A caller can reassign one of their vehicles to a depot id belonging to another tenant, corrupting that tenant's depot rollups and any downstream routing or billing keyed on depot_id.
findings.recommendation: Call depotBelongsTo in update as well, or move the check into the repository so both writers share it.

triage.reason: A composite foreign key (depot_id, tenant_id) would enforce this in the database, but no DDL or migration was provided; per FP-08 that keeps this at probable.
depotId is a request body field carrying only @NotBlank (VehicleController.java:102).

findings.title: Billing webhook signature check returns true when the secret is empty
findings.class: Authentication bypass / control that cannot fail
findings.unaided_label: signatureMatches returns true when secret falsy
findings.evidence: `if (!secret) return true` is the first branch of the verifier. The secret is supplied by nuxt.config.ts:9 as `process.env.BILLING_WEBHOOK_SECRET ?? ''` - an empty string when the variable is unset, which is falsy, so every request verifies. There is no start-up assertion anywhere in the tree that the variable is set (contrast labtrack/labtrack/app.py:33-35, which does exactly that for its signing key). 01.session.ts:4 lists /api/billing/webhook in OPEN_PREFIXES, so no session is required either.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated caller posts {"type":"charge.succeeded","data":{"orderId":...}} and the order moves from draft to scheduled with an attacker-chosen total_cents, and a receipt email is queued - goods shipped with no payment. `charge.refunded` cancels any order by id. A misconfiguration that would normally fail loudly instead fails open and silently.
findings.recommendation: Fail closed: refuse to boot (or return 500) when billingWebhookSecret is empty, and delete the sandbox branch. Emulator environments should carry a real test secret, not no secret.

triage.reason: The route is explicitly exempted from the session middleware at 01.session.ts:4 and is not under CUSTOMER_AREA or STAFF_AREA in 02.authz.ts, so no other layer authenticates it.
The branch is in the shipped handler, gated on a value rather than on an environment flag; nothing removes it from a production build.

findings.title: Order creation is outside the customer-area prefix and takes the customer id from the body
findings.unaided_label: POST /api/orders unguarded; customerId falls back to body
findings.evidence: 02.authz.ts:3 defines CUSTOMER_AREA = '/api/orders/' with a trailing slash and gates with path.startsWith(...). The collection route for server/api/orders/index.post.ts is /api/orders, with no trailing slash. I evaluated the predicate: '/api/orders'.startsWith('/api/orders/') is false, while '/api/orders/abc' is true - so GET and PATCH on a single order are gated and POST on the collection is not. The handler then computes `event.context.session?.customerId ?? body.customerId`, and newOrderSchema (schemas.ts:8) makes customerId a required body field.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated caller creates orders attributed to any customer id, and the response hands back that order's id and share_token. Chained with the webhook bypass above, orders can be created for arbitrary customers and then marked paid.
findings.recommendation: Gate on the resource root rather than the prefix ('/api/orders' with or without the slash, or a route-level guard), and never accept customerId from the body for a signed-in surface. If guest checkout genuinely needs it, bind it to the checkout token that created the customer record.

triage.reason: 01.session.ts only populates a session when a valid cookie is present and returns silently otherwise (lines 29-31, 40-42); it never rejects. No other middleware exists - the server/middleware directory holds exactly these two files.
The comment at index.post.ts:5-8 shows guest checkout was intended, but guest checkout is not the same as accepting any customer id from an anonymous caller.

findings.title: Per-customer order responses are cached by a shared stale-while-revalidate rule
findings.evidence: '/api/orders/**': { swr: 120 } caches the responses of GET /api/orders/{id}, whose body is scoped to one customer by orderForCustomer(id, session.customerId) (db.ts:45-51) and includes note, total_cents and share_token. No cache key, no varies list and no Cache-Control: private accompany the rule; the adjacent '/api/billing/**': { cache: false } (line 32) shows the authors did reason about which routes must not be cached and did not put this one in that class. The 'vary: origin' at line 26 is a response header on a different rule, not a cache key.
findings.impact: Within the 120 second window, the stored body of one customer's order is replayed to any other caller who requests the same order id, exposing the note, the amount charged and the share_token that grants sign-in-free access to the delivery.
findings.recommendation: Set { cache: false } (or Cache-Control: private, no-store) for /api/orders/**, or key the cache on the session cookie explicitly. Caching an authenticated response requires the identity in the key.

triage.reason: Whether Nitro's swr cache key includes the pantry_session cookie is a framework behaviour not established anywhere in this tree; no varies configuration is declared here to settle it. Per the UNKNOWN rule this ships as probable, not confirmed. What would settle it: the Nitro cache options in use, or a two-session integration test against the built server.
The cached body carries share_token and total_cents for a named customer's order.

scope.established_by: matched each routeRules glob against the file routes under server/api; '/api/orders/**' reaches [id].get.ts and [id].patch.ts, and only the GET is cacheable
scope.narrowed_by: pantry-portal/server/middleware/02.authz.ts:20 - the request still needs some valid session, so the reader must be a signed-in customer rather than an anonymous one

findings.title: Order note is escaped on create and written raw on patch, then interpolated into receipt HTML
findings.unaided_label: order.note unescaped in receipt; PATCH writes it unescaped
findings.evidence: renderReceiptHtml escapes every interpolated value except one: item.sku (line 131), order.id (134) and order.share_token (137) go through escapeHtml, and `${order.note}` at line 136 does not. The note column has two writers: index.post.ts:23 applies escapeHtml, and updateOrder (db.ts:94-112) writes patch values verbatim - orderPatchSchema only bounds note to 500 characters (schemas.ts:26).
findings.impact: A customer PATCHes their own order's note with markup, then the charge.succeeded webhook renders it into the receipt HTML stored in outbound_email and sent by the transactional mailer - arbitrary HTML, links and images in an email that carries the merchant's identity, and script in any web view that renders it.
findings.recommendation: Escape at render time rather than at one of the two write sites: wrap `${order.note}` in escapeHtml. Escaping on the way into the database is the pattern that produced this gap.

triage.reason: The only sanitiser in the tree is escapeHtml, and its six call sites (grepped) do not include the patch path or line 136.
The sink is an HTML document assembled as a template literal and stored in an `html` column for a mailer, not a text field.

scope.established_by: grep of escapeHtml call sites (6) against every interpolation in renderReceiptHtml, then the two writers of the note column
scope.narrowed_by: pantry-portal/server/api/orders/index.post.ts:23 - the create path does escape, so only notes written through PATCH carry markup

findings.title: Share token comes from Math.random
findings.class: Insecure randomness for a bearer secret
findings.evidence: Twelve characters drawn from a 33-character alphabet with Math.random(). The doc comment (lines 32-35) states the token lets a household member 'pull up the delivery window without signing in', and [id].get.ts:19 returns it to the client, so it is a standalone credential. Math.random is not a CSPRNG; V8's xorshift128+ state is recoverable from a modest number of observed outputs, and every token minted in the same process is drawn from that one stream.
findings.impact: An attacker who collects a few share tokens (their own orders suffice) can predict tokens issued around the same time and read other customers' delivery windows and order detail without authentication.
findings.recommendation: Use crypto.randomBytes(16) rendered base32/base64url, and treat the token as revocable.

triage.reason: This class is about the predictability of a server-generated value, not about attacker-controlled input.
What the token unlocks is a named customer's delivery slot and box contents.
There is no second factor behind the token: the share URL at db.ts:137 is the whole of the access control.

scope.established_by: single caller of newShareToken (insertOrder), and the two responses that return share_token ([id].get.ts:19, index.post.ts:30)

findings.title: Idempotency keys are stored in one namespace shared by all customers
findings.class: Insecure direct object reference through a cache key
findings.unaided_label: idempotency key not scoped to customer
findings.evidence: The key is the raw Idempotency-Key request header (index.post.ts:14) used verbatim as the storage key in the shared 'idempotency' Redis store (nuxt.config.ts:38). Nothing prefixes it with the customer id or a session identifier, and the stored value is the full creation response including id and shareToken.
findings.impact: Any caller who guesses or replays another customer's Idempotency-Key receives that customer's stored order response, including the share_token. Clients commonly derive these keys from a request UUID, but nothing enforces that, and POST /api/orders needs no authentication at all (see the authz-prefix finding), so this is farmable by an anonymous caller.
findings.recommendation: Namespace the key: `${customerId}:${key}` and reject a cached hit whose stored customerId does not match the caller's.

triage.reason: The key is a request header with no format constraint (index.post.ts:14).
The second principal is another customer of the same portal; the store is one Redis keyspace shared across all of them.

scope.established_by: single caller of recordIdempotent, and the storage declaration it resolves to (nuxt.config.ts:37-39)

findings.title: Session cookie carries no expiry and nothing checks one
findings.evidence: After the MAC check the handler parses the claims and validates exactly one field - cid must be a positive integer (lines 51-54). No exp, iat or nbf is read, and the Session interface (lines 6-10) has no expiry field. Contrast labtrack/labtrack/guards.py:41, which does check exp on its own HMAC token.
findings.impact: A cookie captured once is valid forever: logout cannot invalidate it (there is no server-side record), a password change cannot revoke it, and there is no absolute session lifetime. Because the same cookie also carries `staff: true` (line 59), a stale staff cookie keeps administrative reach indefinitely.
findings.recommendation: Sign an exp claim into the payload, reject expired cookies here, and set an absolute maximum lifetime. Add a server-side session or key-version so revocation is possible.

triage.reason: The cookie is the only credential for /api/orders/*; 02.authz.ts reads event.context.session and nothing else.
There is no server-side session store to fall back on, so this is not a redundant check that is merely absent.

findings.title: The payout amount can be raised after the dual-approval gate has passed
findings.class: Business logic / TOCTOU on an approval control
findings.unaided_label: adjustAmount signal mutates amountMinor after threshold check
findings.evidence: The threshold is evaluated once at line 93 against amountMinor, then the workflow blocks in wf.condition(...,'72h') at line 95. The adjustAmount signal handler installed at line 54 assigns `amountMinor = minor` with no bound, no re-evaluation of approvalThresholdFor and no comparison against the amount that was approved. Execution resumes at line 102 and postEntry is called with the mutated value.
findings.impact: Send a payout just under the currency threshold and it never needs an approver; send one above it, collect two approvals for a small amount, then signal a larger amount during the 72-hour window and it is debited and submitted with the approvals of a different figure. The 50_000_00 ceiling that starter.ts:17 enforces on the initial request is not enforced on the signal, so the mutated amount is unbounded.
findings.recommendation: Capture the approved amount in the approval record and refuse to proceed if amountMinor changed after approval; re-run the threshold check immediately before postEntry; validate the signal payload with the same zod schema as the start request.

triage.reason: postEntry's only refusal is the funding-account floor (ledger.ts:38), which is a balance check, not an approval check.
The signal value arrives from starter.ts:57 as `(await readJson(req)) as { amountMinor: number }` - a cast, not a validation.
The handler is installed unconditionally at line 54 and stays live for the whole workflow, including the whole approval wait.

findings.title: A screening failure is swallowed and the degraded flag it sets is never read
findings.unaided_label: screening catch sets blocked:false; degraded never consulted
findings.evidence: The catch block substitutes `{ blocked: false, listHits: [], degraded: true }` for a real screening result and execution continues to line 86, which only tests screening.blocked. I grepped `degraded` across the service: three hits - the interface field (compliance.ts:14), the value set on success (compliance.ts:42) and this substitution. Nothing reads it. screenBeneficiary throws on any status >= 400 (compliance.ts:33) and on any transport error, so an unreachable or erroring screening service is indistinguishable from a clean beneficiary.
findings.impact: Sanctions screening is bypassed whenever the vendor is down, slow past the 2-minute activity timeout, or returns an error - the condition under which a payment should stop is exactly the condition under which it proceeds. The comment at lines 81-83 makes this a deliberate choice, but the compensating 'exception report' is not implemented in this tree.
findings.recommendation: Treat a screening failure as a hold, not a pass: set blocked=true or route to the approval path, and make degraded a value the workflow branches on rather than a field nobody reads.

triage.reason: No downstream activity re-screens: postEntry, adjustEntry and both rails take the beneficiary as given.
This is not defence in depth that is merely absent - it is the primary control, and its failure arm returns the permissive answer.

The claimed compensating process is a morning exception report described in a comment; per FP-08 an unevidenced external control cannot rule a finding out, and here nothing even writes the record it would read.

scope.established_by: grep of `degraded` (3 hits, zero readers) and read of every branch between the catch and postEntry

findings.title: Sanctions enforcement defaults to advisory, so a list hit never blocks
findings.evidence: `sanctionsMode: process.env.SANCTIONS_MODE ?? 'advisory'`. Its single reader is compliance.ts:40: `blocked: listHits.length > 0 && config.sanctionsMode === 'enforcing'`. With the default in effect, blocked is false no matter how many list hits the vendor returns, and payout.ts:86 - the only consumer of blocked - lets the payout through. The interface comment at config.ts:6 documents both modes; nothing in the tree sets the environment variable or asserts it at start-up.
findings.impact: A deployment that never sets SANCTIONS_MODE runs with sanctions screening in report-only mode while the code reads as though it blocks. Combined with the swallowed-exception finding above, there is no reachable path in this tree on which a beneficiary is refused.
findings.recommendation: Default to 'enforcing' and fail start-up on an unrecognised value; make the mode explicit in deployment config rather than implicit in a `??`.

triage.reason: The dangerous value is the default itself, not attacker input; the rule is about the value's origin and here the origin is a literal in the shipped config.

config.ts is the production configuration module imported by worker.ts, starter.ts and every activity; there is no separate production file that overrides it. A deployment manifest could set SANCTIONS_MODE=enforcing and none was provided, but the assertion reported here is about the shipped default and its single reader, both of which are established in this tree - the environment question is recorded in coverage.open_questions rather than invoked as an exculpation.

findings.title: The payout HTTP API authenticates nothing and validates the signal body not at all
findings.unaided_label: starter API has no auth; /amount takes an unvalidated cast
findings.evidence: The request handler has no token check, no session, no mTLS and no shared secret on any of its three routes: POST /payouts starts a money-moving workflow, POST /payouts/{id}/amount signals an existing one, GET /accounts/{id}/entries reads a ledger. The signal route additionally does `(await readJson(req)) as { amountMinor: number }` at line 55 - a TypeScript cast that performs no runtime validation - while the start route does parse a zod schema. The only stated control is the loopback bind at line 83.
findings.impact: Anything that can open a TCP connection to 127.0.0.1:8410 - the ops-console sidecar, any other container sharing the pod's network namespace, any code-execution foothold in the pod, or any SSRF that resolves to loopback - can start payouts, mutate the amount of a pending one and read ledger entries, with no record of which operator did it.
findings.recommendation: Require an authenticated operator identity on every route (mTLS or a signed service token), record it as the actor, and parse the signal body with the same payoutRequestSchema fields it mutates.

triage.reason: The comment at line 82 names a second principal itself - an ops console sidecar - and that sidecar's own users are not distinguished here; a shared loopback socket inside a pod is not a single-principal boundary.
Under FP-05 an intended exposure moves the finding to whatever sits behind it; behind this one there is no authorization at all, which is the finding.
A service mesh or sidecar policy could authenticate callers, but no mesh config, NetworkPolicy or deployment manifest was provided.

scope.established_by: read every branch of the single createServer callback; the three route tests are the whole surface
scope.narrowed_by: payout-orchestrator/src/starter.ts:83 - server.listen(port, '127.0.0.1') keeps the socket off the pod's external interfaces

findings.title: The rail reference doubles as a callback secret and comes from Math.random
findings.class: Insecure randomness for a bearer secret
findings.unaided_label: newReference uses Math.random and is the callback secret
findings.evidence: `Math.random().toString(36).slice(2, 12)` appended to Date.now() in base 36. The doc comment at lines 17-20 states the rail 'quotes it back on its status callback, so it doubles as the callback secret'. The same value is sent as the primary rail's idempotency-key header (line 30). Both components are guessable: the timestamp is knowable to the second and the suffix is drawn from a non-cryptographic PRNG whose internal state is recoverable from observed outputs.
findings.impact: An attacker who can reach the callback endpoint forges rail status callbacks for real payouts - marking a transfer settled that was not, or the reverse - and can collide the rail idempotency key to suppress or duplicate a submission.
findings.recommendation: Generate the reference with crypto.randomBytes and stop using it as an authenticator: verify callbacks with a signature over the body using a shared secret, and keep the reference as a non-secret identifier.

triage.reason: The callback handler that consumes the reference is not in this tree, so the exploitability of forging one cannot be established here; per the UNKNOWN rule this ships as probable. What would settle it: the service that receives the rail status callback and what it checks.
The defect is the predictability of a server-generated secret, not attacker-controlled input.
The comment states the reference is the callback authenticator, so there is no separate control whose absence would merely be defence in depth.

findings.title: Every payout API response carries Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
findings.evidence: corsOrigin defaults to '*' and is written unconditionally as the first line of the request handler (starter.ts:37), before any routing, so it lands on all three routes and on the 404. Because this API requires no credentials at all, a cross-origin GET is a simple request and needs no preflight to succeed.
findings.impact: Any web page loaded in a browser that can route to the API host reads GET /accounts/{id}/entries cross-origin and exfiltrates ledger data. The wildcard blocks credentialed reads, which is why this is not high, but the API has no credentials to block.
findings.recommendation: Default corsOrigin to the ops console origin and fail start-up if it is unset in production; do not emit the header on routes that return account data.

triage.reason: I checked specifically for a narrowing and there is none: the setHeader at starter.ts:37 is outside the route dispatch, so unlike the classic single-route wildcard this one does apply to everything the server returns.
The response bodies reachable this way are ledger entries with amounts and memos.
There is no credential whose absence would make cross-origin reads harmless - the absence of authentication is what makes them work.

findings.title: The funding floor is enforced by one writer of the balance and not the other
findings.unaided_label: adjustEntry writes balance_minor with no floor check
findings.evidence: postEntry, documented as 'the one way money leaves a funding account' (lines 21-24), takes a FOR UPDATE lock, reads floor_minor and refuses when `balance - amount < floor` (lines 29-40). adjustEntry writes the same column - `UPDATE funding_accounts SET balance_minor = balance_minor + $2` (line 69) - with no lock on the row it reads, no floor read and no refusal. The workflow calls it with a negative delta for the rail fee at payout.ts:113.
findings.impact: The per-transfer rail fee, and any other adjustment, drives a funding account below the floor the ledger claims to defend. The floor is a treasury control; a second writer that ignores it makes the invariant unenforceable rather than merely occasionally violated.
findings.recommendation: Route every balance mutation through one function that reads the floor under FOR UPDATE, or express the floor as a CHECK constraint so both writers hit it.

triage.reason: A CHECK constraint on funding_accounts would enforce this in the database, but no schema was provided; per FP-08's doctrine an unevidenced control is not a HOLDS. The asymmetry inside the file is confirmed regardless.
Both functions update the same column of the same table in the same module; there is no reading on which they touch different state.

scope.established_by: grouped writes by the entity they touch - funding_accounts.balance_minor has exactly two writers - then compared the guards on each

findings.title: A correspondent-rail failure leaves the debit unreversed
findings.class: Missing compensation in a money flow
findings.evidence: The catch at line 125 reverses the debit only when the primary rail failed for a reason other than RailUnavailable. When it was RailUnavailable, the catch falls through without rethrowing and line 133 calls submitCorrespondent outside any try - so a rejection there (submitCorrespondent throws on any status >= 400, rails.ts:68) propagates out of the workflow with postEntry's debit and the fee adjustment still applied.
findings.impact: Funds leave the funding account with no transfer submitted and no reversal booked; reconciliation has to find it by hand. The same branch also carries a double-payment risk: a 503/504 from the primary rail is ambiguous about whether it accepted the transfer, and the fallback resubmits under a different reference (rails.ts:56) so the primary's idempotency key does not deduplicate it.
findings.recommendation: Wrap the fallback in the same compensation, and make the fallback reuse the primary reference as its idempotency key so an ambiguous 504 cannot become two transfers.

triage.reason: Temporal's retry policy (proxyActivities, line 16, maximumAttempts 3) retries the activity, it does not compensate the earlier ones; there is no saga or finally block in this workflow.

Both run under the Admin SDK (line 7-8), so firestore.rules does not apply. cors({origin: true}) on line 72 additionally lets any web page issue the GET from a visitor's browser.
findings.recommendation: Add `adminApi.use(requireIdToken)` and an explicit administrator check on top of it - the token alone is not an admin claim - and replace origin: true with the allowlist the comment says was being avoided.

firebase.json:7 rewrites /admin/** to this function in the shipped hosting configuration; it is not behind a flag or an emulator-only path.

findings.title: The org export callable checks neither authentication nor membership
findings.class: Missing authorization on a privileged export
findings.unaided_label: exportOrgNotes has no auth or membership check
findings.evidence: The handler validates one thing - that request.data.orgId is a non-empty string (lines 89-92) - and then reads up to 5000 notes from any org with the Admin SDK. `request.auth` is never referenced. Contrast api.get('/notes/recent') at lines 47-50, which loads the caller's profile and returns 403 unless orgId is in profile.orgs: the membership check the codebase knows how to write is absent from the route whose docstring says it 'spans every inspector's notes in the org'.
findings.impact: A caller who names an org id receives every field note in it - id, ownerId, status, title and body - as CSV. Because the Admin SDK bypasses firestore.rules, the org-membership rule at firestore.rules:46 does not apply, and this is the widest read surface in the project.
findings.recommendation: Reject when request.auth is missing, then apply the same profile/orgs membership check the /notes/recent route uses, and consider requiring an admin role for a whole-org export.

Note bodies are inspection records naming sites and hazards, and ownerId identifies the inspector.
The limit(5000) at line 94 bounds one response, not which orgs may be named; orgId is a free parameter.

findings.title: The seal endpoint writes the audit trail from client-supplied keys with no membership check
findings.unaided_label: seal writes audits/{orgId}_{seq} with .set() and no org check
findings.evidence: auditId is `${orgId}_${seq}` built from the request body (line 61), and the write is db.doc(...).set(...) - a full overwrite, not create - through the Admin SDK. Its sibling on the same express app, GET /notes/recent, loads the caller's profile and returns 403 when orgId is not in profile.orgs (lines 47-50); this handler performs no such check. firestore.rules:50-54 declares the collection an 'immutable trail written by the audit function with the Admin SDK' and sets `allow write: if false` for clients.
findings.impact: Any authenticated user overwrites any audit record - their own or another org's - by naming its orgId and seq, replacing sealedBy and noteId with values of their choosing, and can seal notes in orgs they do not belong to. The one record intended to be immutable is client-addressable and client-overwritable.
findings.recommendation: Apply the membership check the sibling route uses, derive orgId from the note document rather than the body, use create() so an existing audit id cannot be overwritten, and generate the audit id server-side.

triage.reason: The `allow write: if false` rule at firestore.rules:53 governs client SDK access; this write goes through admin.firestore(), which is exempt from rules by design.
orgId and seq come from req.body via normalizeRequest (line 60); the sanitiser strips characters from orgId but does not check membership, and seq is any number.
set() without {merge:true} is a replace, so this is not an append-only write that merely looks overwriting.

findings.title: Users can write their own role and org membership, which the rules then trust
findings.unaided_label: profiles self-write includes role and orgs
findings.evidence: `allow write: if request.auth.uid == uid` permits a user to write every field of their own profile, and the profile document is what the rest of the ruleset reads for authorization: role() (line 15) returns profile().role and memberOf(orgId) (line 19) tests `orgId in profile().orgs`. Those two functions gate the org write rule (line 43), the org subcollection rule (line 46) and the audits read rule (line 52). The web client already writes this document on first sign-in with a client-supplied orgId (auth.js:28, register at line 35).
findings.impact: Any signed-in user sets their own role to 'admin' and adds any orgId to their own orgs array, then reads and writes that organisation's documents (line 46) and reads the audit trail (line 52). The functions layer inherits the same trust: api.get('/notes/recent') checks membership against this self-written profile (index.js:47-48).
findings.recommendation: Restrict the profile write to the presentation fields and reject changes to role and orgs - `allow update: if request.auth.uid == uid && request.resource.data.role == resource.data.role && request.resource.data.orgs == resource.data.orgs` - and move membership into an org-controlled members collection written by a privileged function.

triage.reason: No custom claims are set anywhere in the tree - I grepped the functions for setCustomUserClaims and there are none - so the profile document is the only source of role and membership.
The rule is unqualified `allow write`, which in Firestore covers create, update and delete of every field.

scope.established_by: traced every rule and handler that reads profile().role or profile().orgs back to the single document the user may write

findings.title: A wildcard org subcollection rule overrides note ownership, and the ownership rule matches nothing
findings.unaided_label: orgs/** read,write for any member; /notes/{noteId} rule is dead
findings.evidence: Two rules claim the same data and only one applies. `match /notes/{noteId}` (lines 35-39) enforces resource.data.ownerId == request.auth.uid on read, update and delete - but the client writes notes to `collection(db, 'orgs', orgId, 'notes')` (notes.js:19), and firestore.indexes.json:12-19 confirms the app queries a `notes` collection, so the top-level path that rule matches holds no documents. What governs the real location is line 46: `allow read, write: if memberOf(orgId)` for every document under an org, with no owner test at all.
findings.impact: Every member of an org reads, edits and deletes every colleague's field notes, including notes.js's updateNote and deleteNote paths. Combined with the self-writable profile above, any signed-in user makes themselves a member of any org and gains that access across organisations. The ownership rule that was written to prevent exactly this is unreachable.
findings.recommendation: Delete the dead top-level rule and put the owner test where the documents live: scope reads to memberOf(orgId) and writes to `memberOf(orgId) && resource.data.ownerId == request.auth.uid`, with an explicit exception for the supervisor role if that is intended.

triage.reason: In Firestore, rules at different paths are independent and access is granted if any matching rule allows it; the ownership rule cannot constrain a path it does not match.
Shared org access might be intended for some collections, but the presence of the ownership rule shows per-note ownership was intended for notes specifically.
memberOf(orgId) narrows the rule to members - but membership is self-assignable (previous finding), so the narrowing does not bind.

scope.established_by: matched each rule path against the collection paths the client actually addresses in notes.js and the collectionGroup entries in firestore.indexes.json

findings.title: Attachment update accepts any signed-in user and drops the size and type checks create applies
findings.unaided_label: storage allow update: if request.auth != null
findings.evidence: Within one match block, three of the four verbs test noteOwner() == request.auth.uid: read (line 12), create (lines 14-17) and delete (line 22). update (line 20) tests only that the caller is signed in. create additionally bounds the object to 15 MB and to `image/.*|application/pdf`; update carries neither.
findings.impact: Any authenticated user overwrites any note attachment in any org - the evidence photographs behind an inspection record - and replaces it with content of any size and any type, including HTML or JavaScript served from the storage host. Overwriting evidence in a compliance record is a tampering primitive; the size gap is an unmetered storage bill.
findings.recommendation: Give update the same three conditions as create. An update is a write of a new object body and needs every check the first write needed.

triage.reason: Storage rules are the whole access control for this bucket path; no function mediates uploads - notes.js:61 calls uploadBytes directly from the browser.
The comment at line 19 explains it as re-uploading after a rotate or crop, which is the intent; the rule as written does not express that intent by any reading.

scope.established_by: read the four verbs of the single match block side by side and listed which conditions each carries
scope.narrowed_by: fieldnotes/storage.rules:6 - the path template still requires a real {orgId}/{noteId}, so the attacker must know or enumerate an existing note id

findings.title: Shared note body is assigned to innerHTML
findings.evidence: Every other field in the same function is written with textContent - heading at line 30 and both field() nodes at lines 9-11 - and note.body alone goes to innerHTML. body is stored verbatim: createNote passes it through unchanged (notes.js:34) and updateNote splats an arbitrary patch (notes.js:45-48); no sanitiser exists anywhere in the project - I grepped for DOMPurify, sanitize and escape across fieldnotes and found none.
findings.impact: Script stored in a note body executes in the browser of anyone opening the share link, which the docstring says a supervisor sends to an external site contact. The victim's session can read and write the org's notes; and because the org subcollection rule lets any member write any note (previous finding), one member can plant the payload in a colleague's note.
findings.recommendation: Render the body as text, or sanitise with DOMPurify immediately before assignment if rich text is required. Add a Content-Security-Policy to the hosting headers - firebase.json:10-15 currently sets only Cache-Control.

triage.reason: body is a user-authored field written from the client with no server-side validation on any path.
innerHTML parses and activates markup; the surrounding code's use of textContent shows the safe sink was available and chosen elsewhere.
There is no CSP: firebase.json's headers block sets Cache-Control on js/css only.

scope.established_by: grep of client-side HTML sinks across the tree (1 hit), then the writers of the note.body field

findings.title: Org export builds CSV by joining raw fields
findings.unaided_label: CSV rows joined with no quoting or escaping
findings.evidence: `[doc.id, note.ownerId, note.status, note.title, note.body].join(',')` with no quoting, no doubling of quotes, no stripping of newlines and no neutralisation of a leading formula character. title and body are free-text fields authored in the app (notes.js:34). The result is handed to the browser as text/csv and saved to disk (share.js:45-50).
findings.impact: A note title beginning with =, +, - or @ becomes a live formula when the export is opened in a spreadsheet, which is the documented path to command execution through DDE prompts. Independently, a comma or newline in any field shifts every later column, silently corrupting a compliance export that someone will rely on.
findings.recommendation: Quote every field and double embedded quotes, strip CR/LF, and prefix a value starting with a formula character with an apostrophe - or emit JSON and convert client-side with a library that does this.

triage.reason: title and body are user-authored note fields with no validation on write.
The declared type is text/csv (share.js:45) and the file is offered as a download, so a spreadsheet is the expected consumer.
Modern spreadsheets prompt before evaluating, which reduces but does not remove the impact, and the field-shifting corruption needs no prompt at all.

scope.established_by: single producer of the csv field traced to its single consumer in the web client

findings.title: Every profile is readable by every signed-in user
findings.evidence: `allow read: if signedIn()` with no org or ownership condition. The document holds displayName, email, role and orgs (auth.js:24-30). Every other collection in the ruleset is scoped by ownership or membership; this one is scoped by authentication alone.
findings.impact: Any account - including one self-registered through auth.js:35 - enumerates the directory: every inspector's email address, their role and the full list of orgs they belong to. That is a mailing list for phishing and a map of which accounts are worth taking over, and it is the reconnaissance step for the privilege-escalation finding above.
findings.recommendation: Restrict reads to the owner and to members of a shared org, and split presentation fields from authorization fields so the former can be shared without the latter.

triage.reason: Email addresses tied to named individuals and their employer are personal data by PRV-01's definition.
The comment at line 28 describes the document as per-inspector identity, not as a public directory.

The second principal is another inspector, and in this project an account can be self-registered (auth.js:35), so the reader need not be a colleague at all. Severity is set to low because the exposure is to authenticated accounts rather than to the public.
